title: AP Macroeconomics
description: Free AP Macroeconomics study guide: 8 units, 320 practice questions, 80 flashcards, quick reference, memory tricks, and a full practice exam. Completely free.

units.name: Basic Economic Concepts

concepts.intro: Scarcity means unlimited wants versus limited resources, forcing every choice to have an opportunity cost.
b: Opportunity cost = value of the next-best alternative given up
Every point on a Production Possibilities Curve (PPC) reflects a trade-off
'There is no such thing as a free lunch' — even 'free' goods have opportunity costs
Sunk costs (already spent, unrecoverable) should NOT factor into future decisions
Explicit costs are direct payments; implicit costs are foregone alternatives (e.g., forgone wages)

concepts.intro: The PPC shows the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with fixed resources and technology.
b: Points on the curve = full/efficient use of resources; points inside = unemployment/inefficiency; points outside = unattainable (currently)
Bowed-out (concave) PPC reflects increasing opportunity cost due to resources not being perfectly adaptable
A straight-line PPC implies constant opportunity cost (perfect resource substitutability)
Outward shift of the entire PPC = economic growth (more resources, better technology, more capital)
A shift favoring one good only (e.g., a technology improvement in just one industry) rotates the PPC on that axis

concepts.intro: Comparative advantage means producing a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer, which is the basis for beneficial trade — even if one party has an absolute advantage in everything.
b: Absolute advantage = producing more output with the same resources (compare total output)
Comparative advantage = lower opportunity cost (compare trade-offs, not totals)
Mutually beneficial trade requires a terms-of-trade price between each party's own opportunity costs
Specialization based on comparative advantage increases total world output
A country can have absolute advantage in both goods but comparative advantage in only one

concepts.intro: The Law of Demand states price and quantity demanded are inversely related, holding all else constant (ceteris paribus).
b: Determinants that shift demand: Tastes, Income (normal vs. inferior goods), Prices of related goods (substitutes/complements), Number of buyers, Expectations (memorize: T-I-P-N-E)
A change in price causes movement ALONG the demand curve (change in quantity demanded)
A change in a determinant shifts the ENTIRE demand curve (change in demand)
Normal goods: demand rises when income rises; inferior goods: demand falls when income rises
Substitutes: price of one rises, demand for the other rises; complements: price of one rises, demand for the other falls

concepts.intro: The Law of Supply states price and quantity supplied are directly related, holding all else constant.
b: Determinants that shift supply: Resource (input) costs, Technology, Taxes/subsidies, Prices of other goods producers could make, Number of sellers, Expectations (memorize: R-O-T-T-E-N)
A change in price causes movement ALONG the supply curve (change in quantity supplied)
A change in a determinant shifts the ENTIRE supply curve (change in supply)
A per-unit tax on producers shifts supply left (up); a subsidy shifts supply right (down)
Improved technology or lower input costs shift supply to the right

concepts.intro: Equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied; government price controls that deviate from equilibrium create shortages or surpluses.
b: Price ceiling below equilibrium price causes a persistent shortage (e.g., rent control)
Price floor above equilibrium price causes a persistent surplus (e.g., minimum wage, agricultural price supports)
A price ceiling above equilibrium or a price floor below equilibrium is non-binding (no effect)
Simultaneous shifts: if both curves shift, one variable (price or quantity) is determinate and the other is ambiguous without more information
Consumer surplus = area below demand, above price; producer surplus = area above supply, below price

keyFacts: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best foregone alternative — not just money spent.
A bowed-out PPC shows increasing opportunity cost; a straight-line PPC shows constant opportunity cost.
Comparative advantage (lowest opportunity cost) — not absolute advantage — determines mutually beneficial specialization and trade.
Price ceilings below equilibrium cause shortages; price floors above equilibrium cause surpluses.
traps: A price change moves you ALONG a curve, not the curve itself — only a determinant shifts the whole curve.
Absolute advantage is about who produces MORE; comparative advantage is about who gives up LESS — trade is based on the latter, not the former.
Sunk costs should be ignored in decision-making, not treated as a reason to 'stick with' a bad investment.
A country can have an absolute advantage in every good and still benefit from trade if comparative advantage differs.

units.name: Economic Indicators & GDP

concepts.intro: The circular flow model shows how money, goods, and resources move between households, firms, the government, and the foreign sector.
b: Households supply factors of production (land, labor, capital, entrepreneurship) to firms via factor markets
Firms supply goods and services to households via product markets, in exchange for spending
Leakages (savings, taxes, imports) remove money from the flow; injections (investment, government spending, exports) add money
For equilibrium GDP, leakages must equal injections: S + T + M = I + G + X
The government and foreign sectors add complexity beyond the basic two-sector household-firm loop

concepts.intro: GDP (Gross Domestic Product) is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given year.
b: Expenditure approach: GDP = C + I + G + Xn (Consumption + Investment + Government spending + Net exports)
Only FINAL goods count — intermediate goods are excluded to avoid double-counting
Only production WITHIN the country's borders counts (GDP), regardless of who owns the resources (contrast with GNP, which is by nationality)
Investment (I) includes business investment in capital and inventories, and residential construction — NOT financial investments like stocks/bonds
Non-market and used-good transactions (housework, illegal sales, resale of used cars) are excluded from GDP

concepts.l: Nominal vs. Real GDP & the GDP Deflator
concepts.intro: Nominal GDP measures output at current prices, while real GDP adjusts for inflation to allow comparison across years.
b: Real GDP = (Nominal GDP / GDP Deflator) × 100
GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100, a price index for all goods in the economy
Real GDP uses constant base-year prices, isolating changes in actual output from changes in price level
If nominal GDP rises but real GDP falls, all the 'growth' was due to inflation, not more output
Real GDP per capita = real GDP divided by population; used to measure living standards over time

concepts.intro: The business cycle describes the recurring pattern of expansion and contraction in real GDP over time.
b: Phases in order: expansion (growth) → peak → contraction/recession → trough → expansion again
A recession is commonly defined as two consecutive quarters of declining real GDP
Peak: economy at/near full employment and maximum output; Trough: output and employment at their lowest point
The long-run trend line represents potential/full-employment GDP; actual GDP fluctuates around it
A recessionary gap occurs when actual GDP < potential GDP; an inflationary gap occurs when actual GDP > potential GDP

concepts.intro: GDP is a useful but imperfect measure of a nation's economic well-being and total output.
b: Excludes non-market production: household labor, volunteer work, unpaid childcare
Excludes the underground/illegal economy (unreported cash transactions, black markets)
Does not measure quality of life, leisure time, income distribution, or environmental quality/externalities
Does not account for the composition of output (e.g., military goods vs. consumer goods) or negative externalities like pollution
GDP per capita can be misleading if income is highly unequally distributed across the population

keyFacts: GDP = C + I + G + Xn is the expenditure approach — memorize each component's exact meaning.
Real GDP = (Nominal GDP ÷ GDP Deflator) × 100 — always adjust nominal figures for price-level changes before comparing years.
A recession is generally two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP; the trough is the low point, the peak is the high point.
GDP excludes non-market activity, used goods, intermediate goods, and purely financial transactions.
traps: GDP counts only FINAL goods, not intermediate goods — counting both would double-count the same value added.
'Investment' in macro means new capital goods and inventory changes, not buying stocks or bonds — don't confuse it with financial investing.
A rising nominal GDP does not necessarily mean the economy is actually producing more; check real GDP to rule out pure inflation.
GNP measures output by a country's citizens/firms anywhere in the world, while GDP measures output within a country's borders regardless of ownership — these are not interchangeable.

units.name: Unemployment & Inflation

concepts.intro: The unemployment rate measures the share of the labor force that is jobless and actively seeking work.
b: Unemployment rate = (Number unemployed / Labor force) × 100
Labor force = employed + unemployed (people who are actively seeking work); excludes discouraged workers and those not seeking work
Labor force participation rate = (Labor force / Working-age population) × 100
Discouraged workers who stop looking for jobs are NOT counted as unemployed, which can understate true joblessness
Underemployed workers (part-time but wanting full-time work) are counted as fully employed, also understating labor market slack

concepts.intro: Economists classify unemployment by its underlying cause, which affects whether it signals a healthy or struggling economy.
b: Frictional: short-term, from workers transitioning between jobs or entering the labor force (natural and generally healthy)
Structural: mismatch between workers' skills/location and available jobs, often from technological change or industry decline
Cyclical: caused by a downturn in the business cycle (falls in a recession, rises in a boom); the only type tied to the business cycle
Seasonal: predictable, recurring unemployment tied to a time of year (e.g., agriculture, holiday retail)
Natural rate of unemployment (NRU) = frictional + structural unemployment (assumes zero cyclical unemployment); economy is at full employment when actual = natural rate

concepts.intro: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level; the Consumer Price Index (CPI) is the most common tool to measure it.
b: CPI tracks the cost of a fixed 'market basket' of goods and services over time relative to a base year
Inflation rate = [(CPI this year − CPI last year) / CPI last year] × 100
CPI can overstate inflation due to substitution bias, quality/new-product bias, and outlet bias
GDP deflator differs from CPI: the deflator covers ALL domestically produced goods (varies basket), CPI covers a FIXED basket of consumer goods (including imports)
Demand-pull inflation is caused by excess aggregate demand ('too much money chasing too few goods'); cost-push inflation is caused by rising input/production costs

concepts.intro: Inflation redistributes wealth and imposes real economic costs, especially when unanticipated.
b: Menu costs: the real resource cost of updating prices
Shoe-leather costs: the cost/effort of holding less cash and making more trips to the bank to avoid inflation's erosion of money's value
Unanticipated inflation hurts lenders/creditors (repaid in less valuable dollars) and helps borrowers/debtors
Anticipated inflation is less costly because it can be built into contracts, wages, and interest rates (nominal rate = real rate + expected inflation)
Inflation hurts people on fixed incomes (e.g., pensions) and savers holding cash; it helps those holding real assets or fixed-rate debt

concepts.l: Real vs. Nominal Values & the Fisher Equation
concepts.intro: Nominal values are stated in current dollars; real values are adjusted for inflation to reflect true purchasing power.
b: Fisher equation: Nominal interest rate = Real interest rate + Expected inflation rate
Real interest rate = Nominal interest rate − Expected (or actual) inflation rate
Real income/wage growth = Nominal income/wage growth − Inflation rate
If inflation exceeds the nominal interest rate, the real interest rate is negative — savers effectively lose purchasing power
Purchasing power of money moves inversely with the price level: as prices rise, each dollar buys less

keyFacts: Unemployment rate = (Unemployed / Labor force) × 100; discouraged workers are excluded from the labor force entirely.
Natural rate of unemployment = frictional + structural unemployment; full employment does NOT mean zero unemployment.
Fisher equation: nominal interest rate = real interest rate + expected inflation.
Unanticipated inflation redistributes wealth from lenders to borrowers; anticipated inflation has smaller real costs.
traps: 'Full employment' means zero CYCLICAL unemployment, not zero unemployment overall — frictional and structural unemployment still exist.

Discouraged workers are NOT counted as unemployed because they've stopped searching, which can make the official unemployment rate understate true labor market weakness — this is a definitional trap, not a data error.
Inflation redistributes income; it does not automatically make everyone poorer — real asset holders and debtors can benefit from unanticipated inflation.
CPI inflation and GDP deflator inflation can differ because CPI uses a FIXED market basket including imports, while the deflator reflects all current domestic output.

units.name: AD-AS Model

concepts.intro: Aggregate demand is the total quantity of real GDP demanded by households, firms, government, and foreigners at each price level.
b: AD curve slopes downward due to three effects: wealth effect, interest rate effect, and foreign trade (exchange rate) effect
Wealth effect: higher price level reduces the real value of savings, so people spend less
Interest rate effect: higher price level raises interest rates (more money demanded), reducing investment/consumption
Foreign trade effect: higher domestic price level makes exports relatively more expensive and imports cheaper, reducing net exports
AD shifts (not movements) come from changes in C, I, G, or Xn — e.g., consumer confidence, tax cuts, interest rate changes, foreign income

concepts.intro: SRAS shows the relationship between the price level and real GDP supplied in the short run, when input prices (especially wages) are sticky.
b: SRAS slopes upward because higher prices increase profits when input costs (wages) are fixed in the short run, encouraging more output
SRAS shifts left (decreases) with rising input/resource costs, negative supply shocks (e.g., oil price spike), or higher business taxes
SRAS shifts right (increases) with falling input costs, productivity improvements, or subsidies to producers
Stagflation = SRAS shifts left, causing simultaneous higher price level (inflation) AND lower real GDP (recession/higher unemployment)
A supply shock is distinct from a demand shock: it moves price level and output in OPPOSITE directions

concepts.intro: LRAS represents the economy's potential (full-employment) output, determined by resources, technology, and institutions — independent of the price level.
b: LRAS is a vertical line at potential/full-employment real GDP (natural rate of unemployment)
In the long run, wages and prices fully adjust, so changes in price level do not affect real output
LRAS shifts only from changes in the quantity/quality of resources, technology, or institutions — the same things that shift the PPC outward
The intersection of AD and LRAS represents long-run macroeconomic equilibrium
Economic growth is shown as a rightward shift of the LRAS curve (and PPC), not a movement along it

concepts.intro: Short-run macroeconomic equilibrium occurs where AD intersects SRAS; this may not coincide with full-employment output on LRAS.
b: Recessionary gap: SR equilibrium GDP < potential GDP (LRAS) — associated with high unemployment
Inflationary gap: SR equilibrium GDP > potential GDP (LRAS) — economy is 'overheating,' unsustainable in the long run
In a recessionary gap, high unemployment eventually pushes wages down, shifting SRAS right until it returns to LRAS (self-correction) — a slow process
In an inflationary gap, rising wages from labor shortages shift SRAS left, raising prices until output returns to LRAS
Policy is often used to speed up this adjustment rather than waiting for the slow, painful self-correction mechanism

concepts.intro: Changes in AD or AS shift the curves and change equilibrium price level and real GDP; the size of the AD shift depends on the spending multiplier.
b: An increase in AD shifts it right, raising both price level and real GDP (in the short run)
A decrease in AD shifts it left, lowering both price level and real GDP
Simultaneous AD and AS shifts: if AD rises and SRAS falls simultaneously, price level definitely rises but real GDP change is ambiguous
The multiplier effect: an initial change in spending leads to a larger shift in AD because one person's spending is another's income
Spending multiplier = 1 / MPS = 1 / (1 − MPC); this determines the horizontal size of an AD shift from a given change in spending

keyFacts: AD slopes down due to the wealth, interest rate, and foreign trade effects — not the Law of Demand's substitution logic.
SRAS slopes up because of sticky input costs; LRAS is vertical at potential GDP, independent of price level.
A recessionary gap is actual GDP < potential GDP; an inflationary gap is actual GDP > potential GDP.
The spending multiplier = 1/(1−MPC) = 1/MPS determines how much an initial spending change shifts AD.
traps: AD's downward slope is NOT the same reasoning as microeconomic demand (substitution among goods) — it comes from the wealth, interest rate, and foreign trade effects.
LRAS does not shift due to a change in price level — only changes in resources, technology, or institutions shift it (same as PPC shifts).

Stagflation (falling output + rising prices) comes from a leftward SRAS shift, NOT from an AD shift — AD shifts move price and output in the SAME direction, supply shocks move them in OPPOSITE directions.
'Full employment' equilibrium (AD = LRAS = SRAS) is a long-run concept; short-run equilibrium (AD = SRAS) can sit above or below potential GDP.

units.name: Fiscal Policy

concepts.intro: Fiscal policy is the use of government spending and taxation, decided by Congress and the President, to influence aggregate demand and stabilize the economy.
b: Expansionary fiscal policy: increase government spending and/or decrease taxes to close a recessionary gap (shifts AD right)
Contractionary fiscal policy: decrease government spending and/or increase taxes to close an inflationary gap (shifts AD left)
Discretionary fiscal policy requires deliberate legislative action; automatic stabilizers work without new legislation
Automatic stabilizers: progressive income taxes and unemployment/welfare benefits that automatically counteract business cycle swings
Fiscal policy directly shifts AD; it does not directly affect the money supply (that's monetary policy)

concepts.intro: Because one person's spending becomes another's income, an initial change in spending leads to a larger, magnified change in real GDP.
b: MPC (marginal propensity to consume) = fraction of extra income spent; MPS (marginal propensity to save) = fraction saved; MPC + MPS = 1
Spending multiplier = 1 / MPS = 1 / (1 − MPC)
Total change in real GDP = initial change in spending × spending multiplier
A higher MPC means a larger multiplier (more of each dollar gets re-spent, generating more rounds of income)
Government spending changes affect AD dollar-for-dollar times the multiplier; tax changes affect AD by less because part of a tax cut is saved, not spent

concepts.intro: Tax changes affect AD indirectly through disposable income and consumption, making the tax multiplier smaller than the spending multiplier.
b: Tax multiplier = −MPC / MPS = −MPC / (1 − MPC)
The tax multiplier is smaller in absolute value than the spending multiplier because the first round of a tax cut is partly saved (only MPC × tax cut is spent)
A tax increase is contractionary (negative effect on GDP); a tax cut is expansionary (positive effect on GDP)
Balanced-budget multiplier: equal increases in G and T raise real GDP by exactly the amount of the spending increase (multiplier = 1)
To calculate total effect: multiply the tax change by the tax multiplier, or the spending change by the spending multiplier, and sum for combined policies

concepts.l: Government Budget: Deficits, Surpluses & the National Debt
concepts.intro: The budget balance is the difference between government revenue and spending in a given year; the national debt is the accumulation of past deficits.
b: Budget deficit: government spending > tax revenue in a given year (must borrow, issuing Treasury bonds)
Budget surplus: tax revenue > government spending in a given year
National debt = the cumulative sum of all past deficits minus surpluses, accumulated over time
Expansionary fiscal policy (more spending/lower taxes) tends to increase deficits; contractionary fiscal policy tends to reduce them
Financing deficits by borrowing can lead to crowding out of private investment (see below)

concepts.intro: Government borrowing to finance deficit spending can raise interest rates and reduce private investment, partially offsetting fiscal stimulus.
b: Crowding out: increased government borrowing raises interest rates (higher demand for loanable funds), which reduces private investment spending
Crowding out reduces the effectiveness of expansionary fiscal policy on real GDP
Supply-side fiscal policy (e.g., cutting tax rates, deregulation) aims to shift SRAS/LRAS right by increasing incentives to work, save, and invest
The Laffer Curve suggests tax revenue can rise OR fall with a tax rate cut depending on where the current rate sits relative to the revenue-maximizing rate
Supply-side policy differs from demand-side fiscal policy because it targets aggregate SUPPLY, not aggregate demand

keyFacts: Spending multiplier = 1/MPS = 1/(1−MPC); Tax multiplier = −MPC/MPS — the tax multiplier is always smaller in absolute value.
Expansionary fiscal policy (↑G, ↓T) targets a recessionary gap; contractionary fiscal policy (↓G, ↑T) targets an inflationary gap.
The balanced-budget multiplier (equal ΔG and ΔT) equals 1 — GDP rises by exactly the amount of the spending increase.
Government borrowing to finance deficits can crowd out private investment by raising interest rates.
traps: A tax cut of $X does NOT shift AD by the same amount as a government spending increase of $X — the tax multiplier is smaller because part of the tax cut is saved, not all spent.
Automatic stabilizers (progressive taxes, unemployment benefits) work WITHOUT new legislation — don't confuse them with discretionary fiscal policy, which requires a new law.
Running a budget deficit in one year adds to, but is not the same as, the national debt — the debt is the cumulative stock, the deficit is the annual flow.
Fiscal policy shifts AD, not SRAS or LRAS directly — only supply-side fiscal policy (tax rate/incentive changes) is aimed at the supply side.

units.name: Money, Banking & Fed

concepts.intro: Money is anything widely accepted as payment, and it serves three key economic functions.
b: Three functions of money: medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value
M1 = currency in circulation + checkable (demand) deposits + traveler's checks — the most liquid measure of money
M2 = M1 + savings deposits + small time deposits (e.g., CDs) + money market mutual funds — less liquid, broader measure
Money must be: durable, portable, divisible, and scarce (limited supply) to function well
Money is NOT wealth itself — it is a claim on wealth/goods, and its value depends on price level (purchasing power)

concepts.l: The Banking System & Fractional Reserve Banking
concepts.intro: Commercial banks create money by lending out a fraction of their deposits, keeping the rest as required reserves.
b: Required reserve ratio (RRR) = the fraction of deposits banks must hold, set by the Federal Reserve
Required reserves = deposits × RRR; Excess reserves = total reserves − required reserves
Banks can only loan out excess reserves — this is the basis of the money-creation process
A bank's simplified balance sheet: Assets (reserves, loans, securities) must equal Liabilities + Net Worth (deposits owed to customers)
When a bank makes a new loan, it creates new checkable deposits, i.e., new money, in the process

concepts.intro: Because each bank in the system re-lends its excess reserves, an initial deposit expands into a much larger increase in the total money supply.
b: Money multiplier = 1 / RRR
Maximum change in the money supply = initial change in excess reserves × money multiplier
The actual multiplier is often smaller than 1/RRR in reality due to cash leakage (holding currency) and banks holding excess reserves beyond the requirement
A higher RRR means a smaller money multiplier and less money creation from a given deposit
This multiplier process explains how the banking system, not just the Fed printing cash, expands the money supply

concepts.intro: The Federal Reserve ('the Fed') is the U.S. central bank, responsible for conducting monetary policy and regulating the banking system.
b: The Fed's dual mandate: maximize employment and maintain stable prices (control inflation)
Structure: Board of Governors + 12 regional Federal Reserve Banks + the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), which sets monetary policy
The Fed is the 'lender of last resort' to commercial banks and regulates/supervises the banking system
The Fed does NOT control fiscal policy (spending/taxes) — that is Congress and the President's role
The Fed's balance sheet: Assets include government securities and loans to banks; Liabilities include currency in circulation and bank reserves

concepts.l: Money Market: Demand & Supply of Money
concepts.intro: The money market determines the nominal interest rate through the interaction of money demand and the Fed-controlled money supply.
b: Money demand slopes downward: at lower interest rates, people hold more money (lower opportunity cost of holding cash) instead of interest-bearing assets
Money demand shifts with: changes in price level, real GDP/income, or expectations — NOT with interest rate changes (those cause movement along the curve)
Money supply is a vertical line, controlled by the Fed independent of interest rate
Equilibrium nominal interest rate is where money demand equals money supply
An increase in the money supply lowers the nominal interest rate (shifts supply right along a fixed demand curve); a decrease raises it

keyFacts: Money multiplier = 1/RRR; maximum money creation = excess reserves × (1/RRR).
M1 (most liquid: currency + checkable deposits) is a subset of the broader M2 (M1 + savings, small time deposits, money market funds).
The Fed's dual mandate is maximum employment and price stability — it is achieved via monetary policy, not fiscal policy.
Money demand slopes down against the interest rate (opportunity cost of holding money); money supply is vertical, set by the Fed.
traps: Banks can only lend out EXCESS reserves, not total reserves — required reserves must stay on hand.
The money multiplier (1/RRR) gives the theoretical MAXIMUM expansion of the money supply; actual expansion is usually smaller due to leakages and excess reserve holding.
The Fed controls the money supply and interest rates (monetary policy); it does NOT set government spending or tax rates (fiscal policy) — these are separate tools with separate policymakers.
A change in the interest rate causes a movement ALONG the money demand curve, not a shift of the whole curve — only price level, real income, or expectations shift money demand.

units.name: Monetary Policy

concepts.intro: The Fed uses three main tools to change the money supply and influence interest rates.
b: Open market operations (OMO): the Fed's primary and most-used tool — buying government securities increases the money supply; selling decreases it
Reserve requirement: raising the RRR decreases the money supply (banks must hold more, lend less); lowering it increases the money supply
Discount rate: the rate the Fed charges banks for short-term loans; lowering it encourages more borrowing/lending, increasing the money supply
Federal funds rate: the rate banks charge EACH OTHER for overnight loans — the Fed targets this rate via OMO, it is not directly set by decree
Interest on reserves: paying banks interest on reserves held at the Fed can also influence how much banks choose to lend out

concepts.intro: Monetary policy targets the money supply and interest rates to influence investment, consumption, AD, and ultimately real GDP and price level.
b: Expansionary (easy money) policy: buy bonds / lower RRR / lower discount rate → increases money supply → lowers interest rates → used to close a recessionary gap
Contractionary (tight money) policy: sell bonds / raise RRR / raise discount rate → decreases money supply → raises interest rates → used to close an inflationary gap
Lower interest rates stimulate investment and interest-sensitive consumption (e.g., durable goods, housing), shifting AD right
Higher interest rates discourage investment and consumption, shifting AD left
Monetary policy operates with a transmission lag: money market changes → interest rate changes → investment/consumption changes → AD shift → real GDP/price level changes

concepts.intro: The loanable funds market shows how the real interest rate is determined by the supply of savings and the demand for borrowing (investment).
b: Supply of loanable funds comes from savings (households, businesses, foreign lenders, government surplus)
Demand for loanable funds comes from borrowers (businesses investing, government financing deficits, consumers borrowing)
Equilibrium REAL interest rate is where supply of and demand for loanable funds intersect
An increase in government borrowing (deficit spending) shifts demand for loanable funds right, raising the real interest rate — this is the mechanism behind crowding out
An increase in private savings shifts the supply of loanable funds right, lowering the real interest rate

concepts.l: Money Market vs. Loanable Funds Market
concepts.intro: The money market determines the NOMINAL interest rate in the short run via money supply/demand; the loanable funds market determines the REAL interest rate via saving/investment.
b: Money market: vertical money supply (set by Fed), downward-sloping money demand → determines nominal interest rate
Loanable funds market: upward-sloping supply of savings, downward-sloping demand for borrowing → determines real interest rate
Monetary policy (Fed action) is best modeled in the money market; fiscal policy/deficit effects are best modeled in the loanable funds market
Both markets are used together on the AP exam to trace: Fed action → money market rate change → loanable funds/investment change → AD shift → GDP/price level
Quantity of money (stock, e.g., $ in the economy) is different from quantity of loanable funds (flow, e.g., $ borrowed/lent per year)

concepts.l: Monetary Policy & the AD-AS Model (Full Chain)
concepts.intro: Monetary policy's effects flow through several markets before reaching output and the price level — the AP exam frequently tests the full causal chain.
b: Expansionary chain: Fed buys bonds → money supply increases → nominal interest rate falls → investment/consumption rises → AD shifts right → real GDP rises, price level rises (closes recessionary gap)

Contractionary chain: Fed sells bonds → money supply decreases → nominal interest rate rises → investment/consumption falls → AD shifts left → real GDP falls, price level falls (closes inflationary gap)
The Phillips Curve shows a short-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment; in the long run it is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment
Easy money policy can worsen inflation if used when the economy is already at/above full employment
A liquidity trap or lag can weaken monetary policy's effectiveness even when the Fed acts correctly

keyFacts: Open market operations are the Fed's primary tool: buying bonds expands the money supply, selling contracts it.
Expansionary monetary policy → lower interest rates → more investment → AD shifts right (used for recessionary gaps).
The money market sets the nominal interest rate; the loanable funds market sets the real interest rate.
Full causal chain: Fed action → money supply → interest rate → investment/consumption → AD → real GDP & price level.
traps: The Federal funds rate is the rate banks charge each other, and the Fed only TARGETS it through OMO — it does not set it by direct decree like the discount rate.
Lowering the required reserve ratio INCREASES the money supply (banks can lend more) — a common sign-error trap.
Contractionary monetary policy raises interest rates and is used to fight inflation, not to fight a recession — don't reverse expansionary/contractionary with fiscal policy sign conventions.
The short-run Phillips Curve trade-off between inflation and unemployment disappears in the long run — the long-run Phillips Curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.

units.name: International Trade & FOREX

concepts.intro: The balance of payments records all economic transactions between a country's residents and the rest of the world.
b: Current account: records trade in goods/services (net exports), net investment income, and net transfers
Capital/financial account: records flows of financial assets — foreign investment, loans, purchases of securities and real estate
By definition, current account balance + financial account balance ≈ 0 (they must offset, since one records why money leaves/enters, the other how it does)
A current account deficit (importing more than exporting) is generally matched by a financial account surplus (net capital inflow financing that deficit)
Trade balance = exports − imports; a trade deficit means imports > exports

concepts.intro: The foreign exchange market determines exchange rates through the supply and demand for currencies, driven by international trade and investment.
b: Demand for a currency comes from foreigners wanting to buy that country's exports or invest in its assets
Supply of a currency comes from that country's residents wanting to buy foreign goods or invest abroad
Currency appreciation: a currency becomes more valuable relative to another (buys more foreign currency)
Currency depreciation: a currency becomes less valuable relative to another (buys less foreign currency)
Exchange rates are determined by supply and demand for each currency in the FOREX market (flexible/floating exchange rate system)

concepts.intro: Several factors shift currency supply and demand curves, changing equilibrium exchange rates.
b: Relative interest rates: higher real interest rates in a country attract foreign investment, increasing demand for its currency, causing appreciation
Relative inflation rates: higher inflation makes a country's goods relatively more expensive, decreasing demand for its currency, causing depreciation
Relative income growth: rising domestic income increases demand for imports, increasing the supply of domestic currency, causing depreciation
Changes in preferences/expectations: if foreign goods or assets become more desirable, this shifts currency supply and demand accordingly
Central bank intervention: buying/selling currency reserves can also directly shift supply or demand in the short run

concepts.l: Effects of Exchange Rate Changes on Trade
concepts.intro: Currency appreciation and depreciation directly affect a country's net exports and, through AD, its real GDP and price level.
b: Currency appreciation makes a country's exports MORE expensive to foreigners and imports CHEAPER for domestic residents → net exports fall
Currency depreciation makes a country's exports CHEAPER to foreigners and imports MORE expensive for domestic residents → net exports rise
A fall in net exports shifts AD left (contractionary effect); a rise in net exports shifts AD right (expansionary effect)
Appreciation of the domestic currency can help fight inflation (cheaper imports, less net export demand) but hurts export-dependent industries
These exchange-rate-driven AD shifts connect FOREX directly to the AD-AS model tested throughout the course

concepts.l: Linking Monetary Policy, Interest Rates & Exchange Rates
concepts.intro: Domestic monetary policy affects interest rates, which in turn affects exchange rates and net exports — an important full-chain reasoning sequence on the AP exam.
b: Expansionary monetary policy → lower domestic interest rates → decreased foreign demand for domestic currency/increased demand for foreign assets → domestic currency depreciates
Currency depreciation → exports cheaper, imports pricier → net exports rise → AD shifts further right (reinforces expansionary policy)
Contractionary monetary policy → higher domestic interest rates → currency appreciates → net exports fall → AD shifts further left (reinforces contractionary policy)
This means exchange rate effects tend to REINFORCE, not offset, the direct effects of monetary policy on AD
Comparative advantage (Unit 1) is the underlying reason why countries engage in the trade being financed and exchanged here

keyFacts: Currency appreciation makes exports more expensive and imports cheaper, reducing net exports and shifting AD left.
Higher relative interest rates attract foreign investment, increasing demand for the currency and causing it to appreciate.
Current account balance and financial account balance offset each other in the balance of payments.
Expansionary monetary policy depreciates the currency, which reinforces (not offsets) the AD-increasing effect of lower interest rates.
traps: Currency appreciation HURTS net exports (cheaper imports, pricier exports) — students often reverse this and think a 'stronger' currency helps exports.
A trade deficit is not inherently 'bad economics' — it is definitionally offset by a financial account surplus (capital inflows), not a sign of an accounting error.
Higher inflation relative to trading partners causes currency DEPRECIATION (less demand for now-less-competitive goods), not appreciation.
The exchange-rate effect of monetary policy reinforces the direct interest-rate effect on AD — it does not work in the opposite direction.

quiz.q: Which of the following is included in the M1 measure of the money supply?
o: Checkable deposits
Small-denomination time deposits
Money market mutual funds
Savings deposits
quiz.e: M1 consists of currency, checkable (demand) deposits, and traveler's checks.

quiz.q: Which of the following is included in M2 but NOT in M1?
o: Currency in circulation
Checkable deposits
Savings deposits and small time deposits
Traveler's checks
quiz.e: M2 equals M1 plus near-monies such as savings deposits, small time deposits, and retail money market funds.

quiz.q: Money serves all of the following functions EXCEPT:
o: Medium of exchange
Unit of account
Store of value
Factor of production
quiz.e: Money's three functions are medium of exchange, unit of account, and store of value; it is not itself a factor of production.

quiz.q: If the required reserve ratio is 20%, what is the value of the money multiplier?
quiz.e: The money multiplier equals 1/rr = 1/0.20 = 5.

quiz.q: A bank receives a new deposit of $1,000 and the required reserve ratio is 10%. What is the maximum amount this bank can loan out?
quiz.e: The bank must hold $100 (10%) as required reserves and can lend out the remaining $900 in excess reserves.

quiz.q: Using a simple money multiplier of 5, an initial deposit of $2,000 can eventually increase the money supply by a maximum of:
quiz.e: Maximum change in money supply = initial excess reserves × money multiplier; with the full $2,000 as excess reserves, 2,000 × 5 = $10,000.

quiz.q: On a bank's balance sheet (T-account), which of the following is classified as a liability?
o: Reserves
Loans
Checkable deposits
Government securities held by the bank
quiz.e: Checkable deposits are owed to depositors, making them a liability; reserves, loans, and securities held are the bank's assets.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a tool the Federal Reserve uses to directly change the required reserve ratio's effect on the banking system?
o: Setting the required reserve ratio
Changing tax rates
Adjusting government spending
Issuing new stock
quiz.e: The required reserve ratio is one of the Fed's three main monetary policy tools, along with open market operations and the discount rate.

quiz.q: If a bank holds more reserves than the amount required, these additional funds are called:
o: Required reserves
Excess reserves
Vault liabilities
Discount reserves
quiz.e: Reserves held above the legally required minimum are excess reserves, which the bank can lend out to create new money.

quiz.q: In the loanable funds market, an increase in government borrowing to finance a budget deficit will most likely:
o: Decrease the real interest rate
Increase the demand for loanable funds and raise the real interest rate
Have no effect on the interest rate
Increase the supply of loanable funds
quiz.e: Higher government borrowing increases the demand for loanable funds, shifting the demand curve right and raising the equilibrium real interest rate.

quiz.q: In the loanable funds market, the vertical axis represents which of the following?
o: Nominal interest rate
Real interest rate
Price level
Quantity of money
quiz.e: The loanable funds market graphs the real interest rate against the quantity of loanable funds; saving and investment decisions are based on real returns.

quiz.q: An increase in household saving, all else equal, will shift the loanable funds market such that:
o: Supply of loanable funds increases and the real interest rate falls
Demand for loanable funds increases and the real interest rate rises
Supply of loanable funds decreases and the real interest rate rises
There is no change in equilibrium
quiz.e: More saving increases the supply of loanable funds, shifting supply right and lowering the equilibrium real interest rate.

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes fractional reserve banking?
o: Banks must hold 100% of deposits as reserves
Banks hold only a fraction of deposits as reserves and lend the rest
Banks cannot make loans
Banks hold no reserves at all
quiz.e: In a fractional reserve system, banks keep a fraction of deposits as required reserves and lend the remainder, which creates new money.

quiz.q: The Federal Reserve System serves as the central bank of the United States. Which of the following is one of its primary responsibilities?
o: Setting minimum wage laws
Regulating the money supply
Collecting federal income taxes
Approving the federal budget
quiz.e: The Fed's core responsibility is to regulate the money supply and implement monetary policy to promote stable prices and full employment.

quiz.q: If the required reserve ratio decreases, the money multiplier will:
o: Decrease
Increase
Stay the same
Become negative
quiz.e: Since the money multiplier equals 1/rr, a decrease in rr increases the multiplier, meaning each dollar of reserves supports more new money.

quiz.q: Which asset is considered the most liquid?
o: Real estate
Cash
A certificate of deposit
Corporate stock
quiz.e: Cash is immediately usable to purchase goods and services with no conversion cost, making it the most liquid asset.

quiz.q: A single bank receiving a new checkable deposit can safely lend out an amount equal to its:
o: Total deposits
Required reserves
Excess reserves
Net worth
quiz.e: A bank can only safely lend its excess reserves, since required reserves must be kept on hand or on deposit with the Fed.

quiz.q: Which of the following would increase the supply of loanable funds?
o: An increase in consumer confidence leading to more spending
An increase in national saving
An increase in government deficit spending
A decrease in foreign investment inflows
quiz.e: An increase in national saving directly increases the pool of funds available to lend, shifting the loanable funds supply curve right.

quiz.q: The banking system as a whole (not just a single bank) can expand the money supply by a multiple of new excess reserves because:
o: Each bank keeps 100% of new deposits as reserves
Loaned money is redeposited into the banking system and re-lent
The Fed prints new currency for every loan
Interest rates always rise with new deposits
quiz.e: As loans are spent and redeposited in other banks, those banks can lend their excess reserves too, multiplying the initial deposit through the banking system.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of money?
o: Store of value
Unit of account
Medium of exchange
Means of production
quiz.e: Money is not a means of production; it functions only as a medium of exchange, unit of account, and store of value.

quiz.q: If the money multiplier is 4, how much in new excess reserves is needed to increase the total money supply by $800?
quiz.e: Change in money supply = excess reserves × multiplier, so excess reserves needed = 800 / 4 = $200.

quiz.q: A decrease in the required reserve ratio set by the Fed would most likely:
o: Decrease banks' lending capacity
Increase banks' lending capacity and the money supply
Have no effect on the money supply
Force banks to hold more reserves
quiz.e: Lowering rr frees up reserves previously required to be held, allowing banks to lend more and expand the money supply.

quiz.q: On a bank's T-account, an increase in loans made by the bank appears as an increase in:
o: Liabilities
Assets
Net worth only
Reserves
quiz.e: Loans are assets to the bank because they represent money owed back to the bank by borrowers.

quiz.q: Which of the following best explains why currency alone (M0-type cash) understates the total money supply?
o: Checkable deposits can also be used to make purchases
Cash cannot be spent
Savings accounts are illegal
The Fed does not track currency
quiz.e: Because checkable deposits function as money (spendable via checks/debit cards), M1 includes them alongside currency.

quiz.q: An increase in the demand for loanable funds, with supply held constant, will:
o: Lower the equilibrium real interest rate
Raise the equilibrium real interest rate
Have no effect on the real interest rate
Only affect the nominal interest rate
quiz.e: An increase in demand for loanable funds shifts the demand curve rightward, raising the equilibrium real interest rate.

quiz.q: Reserves that a bank is legally required to hold and cannot lend out are called:
o: Excess reserves
Required reserves
Vault cash surplus
Discount reserves
quiz.e: Required reserves are the minimum reserves a bank must hold, set by the required reserve ratio, and cannot be loaned out.

quiz.q: Which scenario describes the process of money creation in the banking system?
o: A bank simply prints new currency
A bank lends its excess reserves, which are redeposited and re-lent by other banks
The government mails checks to all citizens
Banks destroy old currency to make room for new
quiz.e: Money creation occurs as loaned funds are redeposited and re-lent throughout the banking system, expanding the money supply beyond the initial deposit.

quiz.q: A rise in national saving relative to investment demand in the loanable funds market would most likely result in:
o: A higher equilibrium real interest rate
A lower equilibrium real interest rate
No change in the interest rate
A shortage of loanable funds
quiz.e: An increase in saving shifts the supply of loanable funds right, which lowers the equilibrium real interest rate given unchanged demand.

quiz.q: Which of the following would be classified as a near-money (included in M2 but not M1)?
o: A checking account balance
A savings account balance
Currency in a wallet
A traveler's check
quiz.e: Savings account balances are less liquid than checkable deposits and currency, so they are near-monies included only in M2.

quiz.q: The required reserve ratio is best defined as:
o: The percentage of deposits a bank must keep as reserves
The interest rate banks charge each other
The percentage tax on bank profits
The ratio of loans to total bank assets
quiz.e: The required reserve ratio is the fraction of deposits that the Fed requires banks to hold in reserve rather than lend out.

quiz.q: If a bank's required reserves are $500 and its total deposits are $5,000, what is the required reserve ratio?
quiz.e: Required reserve ratio = required reserves / total deposits = 500 / 5,000 = 10%.

quiz.q: An increase in consumer confidence that leads households to save less would shift the loanable funds market to result in:
o: A lower equilibrium interest rate
A higher equilibrium interest rate
No change in equilibrium
A surplus of loanable funds
quiz.e: Less saving decreases the supply of loanable funds, shifting supply left and raising the equilibrium real interest rate.

quiz.q: Which best describes the relationship between the required reserve ratio and the potential money supply?
o: They are directly (positively) related
They are inversely related
There is no relationship
The relationship depends on GDP
quiz.e: Since the money multiplier is 1/rr, a lower required reserve ratio means a larger potential expansion of the money supply—an inverse relationship.

quiz.q: A commercial bank's net worth on its T-account is calculated as:
o: Assets minus liabilities
Liabilities minus assets
Assets plus liabilities
Reserves minus loans
quiz.e: Net worth (bank capital) equals total assets minus total liabilities, keeping the balance sheet balanced.

quiz.q: Which of the following is true regarding vault cash?
o: It counts toward a bank's reserves
It is a liability of the bank
It cannot be used to satisfy reserve requirements
It is not part of the money supply calculation
quiz.e: Vault cash, along with deposits at the Fed, counts as reserves that a bank can use to satisfy its reserve requirement.

quiz.q: When the Fed wants to assess whether banks are meeting minimum reserve requirements, it is examining banks' compliance with the:
o: Discount rate
Federal funds rate
Required reserve ratio
Prime rate
quiz.e: The required reserve ratio sets the legal minimum fraction of deposits banks must hold as reserves, which the Fed monitors for compliance.

quiz.q: If total reserves in the banking system equal $2,000 and required reserves equal $1,500, excess reserves equal:
quiz.e: Excess reserves = total reserves − required reserves = 2,000 − 1,500 = $500.

quiz.q: An increase in the amount of currency the public chooses to hold outside of banks (rather than deposit) tends to:
o: Increase the effective money multiplier
Decrease the effective money multiplier
Have no effect on money creation
Only affect M2, not M1
quiz.e: Currency held outside banks cannot be used as reserves to support further loans, which reduces the effective expansion of the money supply.

quiz.q: Which of the following would most directly increase the demand for loanable funds?
o: Firms becoming more optimistic about future profits and investing more
Households increasing their savings rate
A decrease in government borrowing
A decrease in foreign investment demand
quiz.e: Increased investment demand by firms directly raises the demand for loanable funds, shifting the demand curve rightward.

quiz.q: A bank has $10,000 in checkable deposits and the required reserve ratio is 15%. How much must the bank hold in required reserves?
quiz.e: Required reserves = deposits × required reserve ratio = 10,000 × 0.15 = $1,500.

quiz.q: Which of the following are the three main tools of monetary policy?
o: Taxes, spending, transfer payments
Open market operations, discount rate, required reserve ratio
Tariffs, quotas, subsidies
Minimum wage, price ceilings, price floors
quiz.e: The Fed's three primary monetary policy tools are open market operations, the discount rate, and the required reserve ratio.

quiz.q: If the Federal Reserve wants to pursue expansionary monetary policy, it should:
o: Sell government securities
Buy government securities
Raise the discount rate
Raise the required reserve ratio
quiz.e: Buying government securities injects reserves into the banking system, increasing the money supply and lowering interest rates—expansionary policy.

quiz.q: An open market sale of government securities by the Fed will:
o: Increase bank reserves and the money supply
Decrease bank reserves and the money supply
Have no effect on reserves
Increase the required reserve ratio
quiz.e: When the Fed sells securities, it takes money out of the banking system, reducing reserves and contracting the money supply.

quiz.q: The interest rate that banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves is the:
o: Discount rate
Prime rate
Federal funds rate
Real interest rate
quiz.e: The federal funds rate is the rate banks charge one another for overnight loans of reserves, and it is the Fed's primary policy target.

quiz.q: To combat a recessionary gap, the Federal Reserve should implement policy that:
o: Increases interest rates and decreases the money supply
Decreases interest rates and increases the money supply
Raises taxes
Decreases government spending
quiz.e: An expansionary policy lowers interest rates and boosts the money supply, encouraging investment and consumption to close a recessionary gap.

quiz.q: On a money market graph with interest rate on the vertical axis, an increase in the money supply set by the Fed will:
o: Shift the money demand curve rightward
Shift the vertical money supply curve rightward, lowering the interest rate
Shift the money supply curve leftward, raising the interest rate
Cause movement along the demand curve only
quiz.e: An increase in the money supply shifts the vertical supply curve right, and given downward-sloping money demand, the equilibrium interest rate falls.

quiz.q: An increase in real GDP, holding the money supply constant, would most likely cause the money demand curve to:
o: Shift left, lowering interest rates
Shift right, raising interest rates
Remain unchanged
Become perfectly elastic
quiz.e: Higher real GDP increases the need for money for transactions, shifting money demand right and raising the equilibrium interest rate.

quiz.q: The discount rate is best defined as:
o: The rate the Fed pays on reserves
The rate banks charge each other overnight
The rate the Fed charges commercial banks for short-term loans
The rate on 10-year Treasury bonds
quiz.e: The discount rate is the interest rate the Federal Reserve charges commercial banks that borrow directly from it.

quiz.q: According to the quantity theory of money (MV = PQ), if the money supply doubles and velocity and real output remain constant, the price level will:
o: Stay the same
Fall by half
Double
Fall to zero
quiz.e: With V and Q constant, MV = PQ implies P is proportional to M, so doubling M doubles P.

quiz.q: Which best describes the concept of money neutrality?
o: Changes in the money supply affect only nominal variables in the long run
Money has no effect on the economy at all
Money supply changes only affect real GDP
The Fed cannot change the money supply
quiz.e: Money neutrality holds that in the long run, changes in the money supply affect price levels (nominal variables) but not real output or employment.

quiz.q: The real interest rate is calculated as:
o: Nominal interest rate plus expected inflation
Nominal interest rate minus expected inflation
Nominal interest rate divided by inflation
Nominal interest rate times inflation
quiz.e: Real interest rate = nominal interest rate − expected inflation, which reflects the true cost of borrowing in terms of purchasing power.

quiz.q: If the Fed raises the required reserve ratio, banks will have:
o: More excess reserves and greater lending capacity
Fewer excess reserves and reduced lending capacity
No change in lending capacity
Higher required reserves but the same excess reserves
quiz.e: Raising the required reserve ratio forces banks to hold more reserves, leaving fewer excess reserves available to lend, contracting the money supply.

quiz.q: Contractionary monetary policy is used to address which economic problem?
o: High unemployment
Inflation
A recessionary gap
Low interest rates
quiz.e: Contractionary policy raises interest rates and reduces the money supply to slow spending and combat inflation.

quiz.q: On the money demand curve, a movement along the curve (not a shift) would be caused by:
o: A change in the interest rate
A change in real GDP
A change in the price level
A change in the money supply set by the Fed
quiz.e: A change in the interest rate causes a movement along a given money demand curve, whereas GDP or price level changes shift the entire curve.

quiz.q: An expansionary monetary policy would most likely lead to which sequence of events?
o: Money supply increases → interest rates fall → investment rises → AD increases
Money supply decreases → interest rates fall → investment rises → AD increases
Money supply increases → interest rates rise → investment falls → AD decreases
Money supply increases → interest rates fall → investment falls → AD decreases
quiz.e: Expansionary policy increases the money supply, lowering interest rates, which stimulates investment spending and increases aggregate demand.

quiz.q: Which of the following would the Fed most likely do to fight demand-pull inflation?
o: Buy bonds to increase the money supply
Lower the discount rate
Sell bonds to decrease the money supply
Lower the required reserve ratio
quiz.e: Selling bonds withdraws reserves from the banking system, reducing the money supply and raising interest rates to cool inflationary spending.

quiz.q: The velocity of money (V) in the equation of exchange represents:
o: The total money supply
The average number of times a dollar is spent in a given period
The real interest rate
The inflation rate
quiz.e: Velocity measures how many times, on average, a unit of currency is used to purchase goods and services within a specific time period.

quiz.q: If the Fed increases the money supply, in the long run (holding real output constant), the classical/quantity theory predicts:
o: A proportional increase in the price level
A permanent increase in real GDP
A decrease in velocity to zero
No change in any variable
quiz.e: Per the quantity theory, in the long run additional money leads to a proportional rise in the price level rather than real output, consistent with money neutrality.

quiz.q: Open market operations are considered the Fed's most frequently used tool because they:
o: Require congressional approval each time
Allow for quick, flexible, and precise adjustments to bank reserves
Only affect the discount rate
Directly set tax rates
quiz.e: Open market operations can be conducted daily in small or large amounts, giving the Fed precise, flexible control over reserves and the money supply.

quiz.q: A decrease in the discount rate is a signal that the Fed is pursuing:
o: Contractionary fiscal policy
Expansionary monetary policy
Contractionary monetary policy
Supply-side fiscal policy
quiz.e: Lowering the discount rate makes it cheaper for banks to borrow from the Fed, encouraging more lending—an expansionary monetary policy action.

quiz.q: Which of the following best illustrates the money demand curve's downward slope?
o: As interest rates rise, the opportunity cost of holding money increases, so quantity of money demanded falls
As interest rates rise, people want to hold more money
Money demand is unrelated to interest rates
Money demand only depends on the price level
quiz.e: Higher interest rates raise the opportunity cost of holding non-interest-bearing money, reducing the quantity of money demanded.

quiz.q: When the Fed targets the federal funds rate, it primarily adjusts bank reserves through:
o: Changing income tax rates
Open market operations
Setting minimum wage
Adjusting tariffs
quiz.e: The Fed conducts open market operations (buying/selling securities) to adjust the supply of reserves and steer the federal funds rate toward its target.

quiz.q: If investors expect higher future inflation, the nominal interest rate needed to maintain the same real interest rate would need to:
o: Decrease
Increase
Stay exactly the same
Fall to zero
quiz.e: Since real rate = nominal rate − expected inflation, higher expected inflation requires a higher nominal rate to keep the real rate unchanged.

quiz.q: A decrease in money demand, with the money supply held constant, would cause the equilibrium interest rate to:
o: Rise
Fall
Stay the same
Become undefined
quiz.e: A leftward shift in money demand, with a fixed vertical money supply, lowers the equilibrium interest rate.

quiz.q: Which policy combination would be considered inconsistent (working against each other)?
o: Expansionary fiscal policy and expansionary monetary policy
Contractionary fiscal policy and expansionary monetary policy
Expansionary fiscal policy paired with tax cuts
Contractionary monetary policy during high inflation
quiz.e: Contractionary fiscal policy reduces AD while expansionary monetary policy increases it, so the two work against each other and can offset.

quiz.q: The Fed's dual mandate refers to its goals of promoting:
o: Low taxes and balanced budgets
Price stability and maximum employment
High exchange rates and trade surpluses
Government spending and low unemployment
quiz.e: The Federal Reserve's dual mandate is to pursue stable prices (low inflation) and maximum sustainable employment.

quiz.q: If the Fed lowers the required reserve ratio, the money multiplier will:
o: Increase
Decrease
Stay the same
Become negative
quiz.e: Since the money multiplier is 1/rr, lowering the required reserve ratio increases the multiplier, amplifying the effect of new reserves.

quiz.q: An increase in the price level, holding real GDP constant, would shift the money demand curve:
o: Leftward, because less money is needed for transactions
Rightward, because more nominal money is needed for the same transactions
It would not shift; only movement occurs
Downward along the same curve
quiz.e: A higher price level means more dollars are needed to buy the same quantity of goods, increasing money demand and shifting it rightward.

quiz.q: Which of the following actions would be classified as contractionary monetary policy?
o: Lowering the discount rate
Buying government securities
Raising the required reserve ratio
Lowering the required reserve ratio
quiz.e: Raising the required reserve ratio reduces banks' lending capacity, decreasing the money supply—an example of contractionary monetary policy.

quiz.q: In the short run, an unexpected increase in the money supply is likely to:
o: Have no effect on real output
Lower interest rates and stimulate real GDP growth
Immediately cause proportional inflation with no real effects
Decrease aggregate demand
quiz.e: In the short run, money is not neutral: an increase in money supply lowers interest rates, stimulating investment and increasing real GDP.

quiz.q: The classical dichotomy separates variables into which two categories?
o: Fiscal and monetary variables
Real and nominal variables
Domestic and foreign variables
Short-run and long-run variables only
quiz.e: The classical dichotomy divides the economy into real variables (output, employment) and nominal variables (price level), which money supply changes affect only in the long run.

quiz.q: Which of the following would most likely occur if the Fed simultaneously buys bonds and lowers the discount rate?
o: Contraction of the money supply
Expansion of the money supply
No net effect on the money supply
A rise in the required reserve ratio
quiz.e: Both actions—buying bonds and lowering the discount rate—inject reserves and encourage borrowing, expanding the money supply.

quiz.q: A steeper (less elastic) money demand curve implies that a given shift in money supply will result in:
o: A smaller change in the interest rate
A larger change in the interest rate
No change in the interest rate
An undefined interest rate change
quiz.e: With a steeper (more inelastic) money demand curve, a given shift in money supply produces a larger change in the equilibrium interest rate.

quiz.q: The equation of exchange (MV = PQ) is used primarily to explain the relationship between:
o: Money supply, its velocity, price level, and real output
Government spending and taxation
Exports and imports
Interest rates and unemployment
quiz.e: MV = PQ relates the money supply and its velocity to nominal GDP, which equals the price level times real output.

quiz.q: Which of the following is true about the money supply curve on a standard money market graph?
o: It is upward sloping
It is downward sloping
It is vertical, since the Fed sets the quantity directly
It shifts only in response to interest rate changes
quiz.e: The money supply curve is vertical because the Fed controls the quantity of money directly, independent of the interest rate.

quiz.q: If the Fed wants to lower the federal funds rate, it will most likely:
o: Sell government securities to reduce reserves
Buy government securities to increase reserves
Raise the required reserve ratio
Raise the discount rate
quiz.e: Buying securities increases bank reserves, increasing the supply of federal funds and pushing the federal funds rate down toward the Fed's target.

quiz.q: During a period of stagflation (high inflation and high unemployment), the Fed faces a policy dilemma because:
o: Expansionary policy would worsen inflation while contractionary policy would worsen unemployment
There is no trade-off in this situation
Monetary policy has no effect during stagflation
Fiscal policy is the only tool available
quiz.e: Stagflation creates a dilemma: expansionary policy could reduce unemployment but worsen inflation, while contractionary policy could reduce inflation but worsen unemployment.

quiz.q: An increase in banks' excess reserves due to Fed action (e.g., an open market purchase) allows the banking system to:
o: Decrease the money supply through the multiplier process
Increase the money supply through the multiplier process
Have no effect on the money supply
Only affect the discount rate
quiz.e: New excess reserves can be lent out and redeposited repeatedly, expanding the money supply by a multiple of the initial injection.

quiz.q: Which best describes the transmission mechanism of monetary policy?
o: Money supply change → interest rate change → investment/consumption change → change in real GDP and price level
Money supply change → immediate change in tax rates
Interest rate change → immediate change in exchange rates only
Money supply has no transmission mechanism
quiz.e: Monetary policy works through a chain: changing the money supply changes interest rates, which changes investment and consumption, ultimately affecting real GDP and the price level.

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes interest on reserves as a monetary policy tool?
o: The rate the Fed pays banks on reserves held at the Fed, which can be raised to encourage banks to hold more reserves and lend less
A tax on excess bank profits
The rate banks charge consumers for loans
A tool used only by fiscal policymakers
quiz.e: By raising the interest rate paid on reserves, the Fed can encourage banks to hold more reserves rather than lend them out, tightening the money supply.

quiz.q: A country has an absolute advantage in producing a good when it:
o: Can produce the good at a lower opportunity cost than another country
Can produce more of the good using the same resources than another country
Only produces that good
Imports the good from another country
quiz.e: Absolute advantage means being able to produce more output (or use fewer resources) than another producer, regardless of opportunity cost.

quiz.q: Country X can produce 8 cars or 4 boats; Country Y can produce 6 cars or 6 boats, with equivalent resources. Which country has the comparative advantage in boats?
o: Country X, since its opportunity cost of a boat is lower
Country Y, since its opportunity cost of a boat is lower
Country X, since it has an absolute advantage in boats
Neither, because they can produce the same amount of boats
quiz.e: Country X's opportunity cost of a boat is 2 cars; Country Y's opportunity cost of a boat is only 1 car. Country Y gives up less, so it has the comparative advantage in boats.

quiz.q: Mutually beneficial terms of trade between two countries must lie:
o: Outside both countries' opportunity cost ratios
Between the two countries' domestic opportunity cost ratios
Equal to one country's opportunity cost exactly
Below both countries' opportunity costs
quiz.e: For trade to benefit both nations, the agreed terms of trade must fall between each country's own opportunity cost ratio for the goods traded.

quiz.q: An increase in the value of the U.S. dollar relative to the euro is called dollar:
o: Depreciation
Appreciation
Inflation
Devaluation by law
quiz.e: When a currency's value rises relative to another currency, it is called appreciation; a fall in value is depreciation.

quiz.q: If the U.S. dollar appreciates against the euro, U.S. exports to Europe will likely:
o: Increase, because they become cheaper for Europeans
Decrease, because they become more expensive for Europeans
Stay the same
Immediately double
quiz.e: Dollar appreciation makes U.S. goods priced in dollars more expensive for foreign buyers, reducing the quantity of U.S. exports demanded.

quiz.q: An increase in the U.S. real interest rate relative to other countries would most likely cause the dollar to:
o: Depreciate, as foreign capital leaves the U.S.
Appreciate, as foreign investors demand more dollars to invest in U.S. assets
Have no effect on the exchange rate
Only affect the current account, not the exchange rate
quiz.e: Higher U.S. interest rates attract foreign investment, increasing demand for dollars in the FOREX market and causing the dollar to appreciate.

quiz.q: The balance of payments is composed of which two main accounts?
o: The trade account and the tax account
The current account and the capital/financial account
The fiscal account and monetary account
The import account and export account
quiz.e: A country's balance of payments records transactions in the current account (goods, services, income, transfers) and the capital/financial account (asset flows).

quiz.q: A current account deficit must be offset by which of the following, assuming the balance of payments balances overall?
o: A capital/financial account deficit of equal size
A capital/financial account surplus of equal size
A decrease in foreign exchange reserves only
A trade surplus in the same period
quiz.e: Since the overall balance of payments must balance, a current account deficit is offset by a capital/financial account surplus of roughly equal size.

quiz.q: Which of the following would increase the supply of dollars in the foreign exchange market?
o: Americans wanting to buy more European goods
Europeans wanting to buy more American goods
An increase in the U.S. interest rate
An increase in U.S. exports
quiz.e: When Americans want to purchase foreign goods or assets, they supply dollars (to obtain foreign currency), increasing the supply of dollars in FOREX markets.

quiz.q: Which of the following would increase the demand for dollars in the foreign exchange market?
o: U.S. consumers buying more imported goods
Foreign investors seeking to buy U.S. government bonds
A decrease in U.S. interest rates
An increase in U.S. inflation relative to other countries
quiz.e: Foreign investors must acquire dollars to purchase U.S. assets like bonds, which increases the demand for dollars in the foreign exchange market.

quiz.q: If a country's currency depreciates, its net exports will most likely:
o: Decrease, because imports become relatively cheaper
Increase, because its exports become relatively cheaper and imports more expensive
Stay exactly the same
Become impossible to calculate
quiz.e: Depreciation makes a country's exports cheaper for foreigners and imports more expensive for domestic buyers, which tends to increase net exports.

quiz.q: Relatively higher inflation in the U.S. compared to its trading partners would most likely cause the dollar to:
o: Appreciate, as U.S. goods become more competitive
Depreciate, as U.S. goods become less competitive and demand for dollars falls
Remain fixed regardless of inflation
Only affect the capital account
quiz.e: Higher relative inflation makes U.S. goods less competitive abroad, reducing foreign demand for dollars and causing the dollar to depreciate.

quiz.q: Comparative advantage is determined by comparing:
o: Absolute levels of output between countries
Opportunity costs of production between countries
Population sizes of countries
Currency exchange rates between countries
quiz.e: Comparative advantage is based on which producer has the lower opportunity cost of producing a good, not on absolute output levels.

quiz.q: A U.S. trade deficit means that:
o: The value of U.S. exports exceeds the value of U.S. imports
The value of U.S. imports exceeds the value of U.S. exports
The U.S. has a balanced trade account
The U.S. dollar is automatically appreciating
quiz.e: A trade deficit occurs when a country's imports of goods and services exceed its exports.

quiz.q: In the foreign exchange market, the equilibrium exchange rate is determined by:
o: Government price controls only
The intersection of the supply and demand for a currency
Fixed rules set by the World Trade Organization
The interest rate in the exporting country alone
quiz.e: Like other markets, the exchange rate is determined where the quantity of a currency supplied equals the quantity demanded.

quiz.q: Which of the following would most likely cause the supply of euros in the foreign exchange market to increase?
o: Europeans wanting to buy more American goods and assets
Americans wanting to buy more European goods and assets
An increase in European interest rates
A decrease in American demand for imports
quiz.e: When Europeans want to buy American goods or assets, they supply euros (to obtain dollars), increasing the supply of euros in the FOREX market.

quiz.q: If two countries specialize according to comparative advantage and then trade, total world output will:
o: Decrease
Increase
Remain exactly the same
Become impossible to measure
quiz.e: Specialization based on comparative advantage allows for more efficient use of resources, increasing total combined output and enabling mutually beneficial trade.

quiz.q: A capital/financial account surplus indicates that:
o: A country is a net borrower from the rest of the world, receiving more foreign investment than it sends abroad
A country is exporting more goods than it imports
A country has no trade with other nations
A country's currency has depreciated
quiz.e: A capital/financial account surplus means more foreign investment is flowing into the country than the country is investing abroad, making it a net borrower.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of a current account transaction?
o: A foreign company purchasing U.S. Treasury bonds
A U.S. company purchasing a factory in Mexico
A U.S. consumer purchasing an imported television
A U.S. bank issuing a loan to a foreign government
quiz.e: Purchases of goods and services, like an imported television, are recorded in the current account, whereas asset and investment purchases go in the capital/financial account.

quiz.q: An increase in foreign demand for U.S. exports will, in the foreign exchange market, cause:
o: The demand for dollars to increase, appreciating the dollar
The supply of dollars to increase, depreciating the dollar
No change in the dollar's value
The demand for dollars to decrease
quiz.e: Foreign buyers need dollars to purchase U.S. exports, so increased export demand raises the demand for dollars and causes the dollar to appreciate.

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes speculation's role in the foreign exchange market?
o: Speculation has no effect on exchange rates
Expectations of future currency appreciation can increase current demand for that currency
Speculators are prohibited from trading currency
Speculation only affects the current account
quiz.e: If traders expect a currency to appreciate, they buy it now in anticipation of profit, increasing current demand and often causing the currency to appreciate.

quiz.q: A country whose opportunity cost of producing wheat is lower than another country's should, according to the theory of comparative advantage:
o: Avoid producing wheat entirely
Specialize in and export wheat
Import wheat instead of producing it
Produce wheat only for domestic consumption
quiz.e: A country with a comparative advantage (lower opportunity cost) in a good should specialize in producing and exporting that good.

quiz.q: If the required terms of trade fall exactly on one country's own opportunity cost ratio, that country would:
o: Gain significantly from trade
Gain nothing from trade at that exact rate
Be forced to stop production entirely
Automatically run a trade deficit
quiz.e: If terms of trade equal a country's own domestic opportunity cost, that country is indifferent between trading and producing domestically—it gains nothing at that exact rate.

quiz.q: Which of the following would most likely lead to a depreciation of the Japanese yen relative to the U.S. dollar?
o: An increase in Japanese interest rates relative to U.S. rates
An increase in U.S. demand for Japanese goods
An increase in Japanese demand for U.S. goods and assets
A decrease in U.S. inflation relative to Japan
quiz.e: If Japanese residents want more U.S. goods and assets, they supply yen to obtain dollars, increasing yen supply and causing the yen to depreciate.

quiz.q: The net export effect of monetary policy suggests that an expansionary monetary policy that lowers domestic interest rates will:
o: Cause the domestic currency to appreciate and decrease net exports
Cause the domestic currency to depreciate and increase net exports
Have no effect on the currency or net exports
Cause an immediate trade deficit
quiz.e: Lower domestic interest rates reduce foreign demand for domestic assets, depreciating the currency, which makes exports cheaper and increases net exports.

quiz.q: Which best explains why voluntary trade between two countries can benefit both, even if one has an absolute advantage in producing everything?
o: Absolute advantage guarantees gains from trade
Comparative advantage, based on differing opportunity costs, still allows for mutually beneficial specialization
Trade is only beneficial if resources are identical
Gains from trade require government subsidies
quiz.e: Even without an absolute advantage, a country can have a comparative advantage due to lower opportunity cost, allowing both countries to gain from specialization and trade.

quiz.q: A tariff placed on imported steel would most likely:
