quiz.e: Keynesian economics generally supports active fiscal policy intervention to close recessionary or inflationary gaps rather than waiting for slow wage/price adjustments.

quiz.q: If a country simultaneously cuts government spending and lowers tax rates for businesses to encourage investment, which combined effect on AD and AS is most likely?
o: AD moves left (from the spending cut) while AS could move right (from the investment incentive) — a mixed policy stance
Both AD and AS shift left
Both AD and AS shift right with certainty
Neither curve is affected
quiz.e: The spending cut is contractionary for AD, while the business tax incentive is a supply-side policy aiming to shift AS right — together forming a mixed fiscal stance.

quiz.q: Which best describes the difference between a cyclical deficit and a structural deficit?
o: A cyclical deficit results from automatic stabilizers during a downturn; a structural deficit persists even at full employment due to policy choices
They are the same thing
A structural deficit only occurs during recessions
A cyclical deficit never disappears
quiz.e: The cyclical deficit reflects temporary revenue/spending changes tied to the business cycle, while the structural deficit would remain even if the economy were at full employment, reflecting underlying spending/tax policy.

quiz.q: If Congress increases spending on defense by $40 billion while MPC = 0.8, what is the total change in real GDP, ignoring crowding out?
o: $40 billion
$50 billion
$200 billion
$32 billion
quiz.e: Multiplier = 1/(1−0.8) = 5; total change in GDP = $40B × 5 = $200 billion.

quiz.q: Which best explains why some economists argue fiscal policy is less effective in a very open economy with high capital mobility?
o: Higher interest rates from government borrowing can attract foreign capital, appreciating the currency and reducing net exports, offsetting some of the AD boost
Open economies cannot run budget deficits
Fiscal policy has no interest rate effects
Currency appreciation always increases net exports
quiz.e: In an open economy, government borrowing-driven higher interest rates can attract foreign capital, appreciate the currency, and reduce net exports — a form of crowding out that partially offsets the AD increase.

flashcards.d: Anything generally accepted as payment for goods/services and repayment of debt; must serve as medium of exchange, unit of account, and store of value.
The most liquid measure of money: currency in circulation, checkable (demand) deposits, and traveler's checks.
M1 plus near-monies: savings deposits, small time deposits (CDs under $100k), and retail money market mutual funds.
The fraction of deposits banks must hold as reserves (not loan out), set by the Federal Reserve.
Reserves a bank holds beyond the required amount; these are the funds available for a bank to loan out.
1/rr — the maximum factor by which the money supply can expand from a new deposit of excess reserves through the banking system.
The central bank of the United States, responsible for regulating the money supply and implementing monetary policy.
A simplified balance sheet showing a bank's assets (reserves, loans, securities) on the left and liabilities (deposits, net worth) on the right, used to track how a deposit changes the money supply.
A banking system in which banks keep only a fraction of deposits as reserves and lend out the rest, creating new money in the process.
The market where savers supply funds and borrowers (investors) demand funds; the real interest rate is the price that equilibrates saving and investment.
The Fed's three main tools: open market operations, the discount rate, and the required reserve ratio (also interest on reserves).
The Fed's buying (expansionary) or selling (contractionary) of government securities to change bank reserves and the money supply; the most frequently used tool.
The interest rate the Fed charges commercial banks for short-term loans; lowering it is expansionary, raising it is contractionary.
The interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves; the Fed targets this rate through open market operations.
The Fed increases the money supply (buys bonds, lowers discount rate/rr) to lower interest rates, increase investment/consumption, and combat a recessionary gap.
The Fed decreases the money supply (sells bonds, raises discount rate/rr) to raise interest rates, reduce spending, and combat inflation.
Graph with interest rate on the vertical axis and quantity of money on the horizontal axis; money demand slopes downward, money supply is vertical (set by the Fed).
MV = PQ, where M is money supply, V is velocity of money, P is price level, and Q is real output; in the long run, changes in M cause proportional changes in P (money neutrality).
Real interest rate = nominal interest rate − expected inflation; investment decisions depend on the real interest rate.
The long-run classical concept that changes in the money supply affect only nominal variables (price level) and not real variables (real GDP, employment).
The ability of a producer to make a good using fewer resources/inputs than another producer.
The ability of a producer to make a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer; the basis for mutually beneficial trade.
The rate at which two countries agree to exchange goods; mutually beneficial terms lie between the two countries' opportunity cost ratios.
A record of all transactions between a country's residents and the rest of the world, composed of the current account and the capital/financial account.
Records trade in goods and services (net exports), net income, and net transfers; a trade deficit means imports exceed exports.
Records international purchases of assets, such as foreign direct investment and portfolio investment; a surplus here offsets a current account deficit.
The market where currencies are traded; the exchange rate is determined by the supply and demand for a currency.
An increase in the value of one currency relative to another, making exports more expensive and imports cheaper.
A decrease in the value of one currency relative to another, making exports cheaper and imports more expensive.
Relative interest rates, relative income/growth, relative price levels (inflation), and speculation/expectations shift currency supply and demand curves in the FOREX market.
The value of the next-best alternative given up when a choice is made; the true cost of any decision.
A graph showing the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with fixed resources and technology.
The ability to produce more output of a good than another producer using the same amount of resources.
The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer; the true basis for beneficial trade.
As the price of a good rises, quantity demanded falls, and vice versa, holding all else constant.
As the price of a good rises, quantity supplied rises, and vice versa, holding all else constant.
A legal maximum price; if set below equilibrium, it is binding and causes a shortage.
A legal minimum price; if set above equilibrium, it is binding and causes a surplus.
Non-price factors — income, tastes, prices of related goods, expectations, and number of buyers — that shift the entire demand curve.
A cost already incurred and unrecoverable; it should not influence rational future decisions.
A diagram showing how money, goods, and resources flow between households, firms, government, and the foreign sector.
The total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given period.
A method of calculating GDP as C + I + G + Xn (consumption + investment + government spending + net exports).
GDP measured using current-year prices, not adjusted for inflation.
GDP adjusted for changes in the price level, allowing accurate comparison of output across years.
A price index measuring the average price level of all goods produced domestically, used to convert nominal GDP to real GDP.
The recurring pattern of expansion, peak, contraction (recession), and trough in real GDP over time.
A significant decline in economic activity, commonly identified as two or more consecutive quarters of falling real GDP.
The total output produced by a country's citizens and firms, regardless of where in the world production occurs.
GDP excludes non-market activity, leisure, income distribution, environmental costs, and the underground economy, limiting its use as a welfare measure.
The percentage of the labor force that is jobless, available for work, and actively seeking employment: (Unemployed / Labor Force) × 100.
A person who wants a job but has stopped actively searching and is therefore excluded from the labor force and unemployment count.
Short-term unemployment from workers transitioning between jobs or entering the labor force for the first time.
Unemployment caused by a mismatch between workers' skills and the skills employers demand, often due to technological change or industry decline.
Unemployment caused by a downturn in the business cycle, rising during recessions and falling during expansions.
The unemployment rate at full employment, consisting only of frictional and structural unemployment, with zero cyclical unemployment.
A price index measuring the cost of a fixed market basket of goods and services purchased by a typical urban consumer, used to track inflation.
The formula stating that the nominal interest rate equals the real interest rate plus the expected inflation rate.
Inflation that is not expected, which redistributes wealth from lenders/savers to borrowers by eroding the real value of fixed nominal payments.
A combination of stagnant output (high unemployment) and high inflation occurring simultaneously, often caused by a negative supply shock.
The total quantity of real GDP that all buyers in an economy are willing to purchase at each price level; slopes downward due to wealth, interest rate, and foreign trade effects.
An upward-sloping curve showing total output firms will produce at each price level in the short run, when input costs like wages are sticky.
A vertical curve at potential (full-employment) GDP, representing the economy's maximum sustainable output independent of the price level.
A situation where short-run equilibrium real GDP is below potential GDP, associated with cyclical unemployment.
A situation where short-run equilibrium real GDP exceeds potential GDP, associated with rising inflationary pressure.
The factor by which an initial change in spending is multiplied to determine the total change in real GDP; equals 1/(1−MPC) = 1/MPS.
The fraction of an additional dollar of income that a household spends on consumption rather than saving.
Inflation caused by an increase in aggregate demand pulling the price level upward as the economy moves along SRAS.
Inflation caused by a leftward shift in SRAS due to rising production costs, which raises prices while lowering real output.
The long-run process by which wages and prices adjust to eliminate recessionary or inflationary gaps, moving the economy back to potential GDP without policy intervention.
The use of government spending and taxation, decided by Congress and the President, to influence aggregate demand and the overall economy.
Increased government spending and/or decreased taxes used to raise AD and close a recessionary gap.
Decreased government spending and/or increased taxes used to reduce AD and close an inflationary gap.
The factor (−MPC/MPS) by which a change in taxes affects total GDP; smaller in absolute value than the spending multiplier because part of any tax change is saved.
The multiplier effect when government spending and taxes change by the same amount; always equal to 1.
A deficit is the annual shortfall when spending exceeds revenue (a flow); the national debt is the cumulative total of past deficits minus surpluses (a stock).
The reduction in private investment caused by government borrowing driving up interest rates in the loanable funds market.
Government programs like progressive taxes and unemployment benefits that automatically counteract business cycle swings without new legislation.
